title: Materials and Manufacturing
description: What materials are made of, how they fail, how things are shaped, and how to choose a material and process together.
audience: Adults who know stress and strain and basic chemistry and want to understand why parts are made of what they are and how.
outcomes: You'll be able to read a stress-strain curve and name the properties it shows.
You'll be able to use the lever rule on steel and explain heat treatment.
You'll be able to compute casting, forming and machining quantities.
You'll be able to choose a material with a performance index.

lessons.title: What a tensile test tells you
lessons.objective: Read strength, stiffness, ductility and toughness from a stress-strain curve and compute elongation and reduction in area.

concepts.title: Yield and ultimate strength
concepts.summary: Yield is where permanent deformation starts; ultimate strength is the highest engineering stress before necking.

concepts.title: Ductility
concepts.summary: How far a material stretches before it breaks, reported as percent elongation or reduction in area.

concepts.title: Toughness
concepts.summary: The energy absorbed per volume up to fracture, the area under the stress-strain curve.

misconceptions: Learners treat strong and stiff as the same. Stiffness is the slope in the elastic region; strength is the stress at yield or fracture.
Learners treat hard, strong and tough as synonyms. Hardness resists indentation, strength resists load, toughness absorbs energy.
Learners think the curve falling after the peak means the metal is weakening. It is the engineering stress dropping because area shrinks at the neck.
sequence: Pull a bar and plot load against stretch, then convert to stress and strain (assumed from the Engineering course).
Elastic region: slope E; unload and it returns.
Yield and the 0.2 percent offset method.
Ductility numbers: elongation, reduction in area.
Toughness as area; compare steel, glass and rubber.
examples: Bar 10 mm diameter, gauge length 50 mm, fractures at 60 mm: elongation 20 percent.
Fracture diameter 7 mm: area 78.54 to 38.48 mm^2, reduction 51.0 percent.
Annealed low-carbon steel yields around 250 MPa and ruptures near 400 MPa; glass shows no plastic region at all.

figures.shows: stress_strain cases for steel, aluminium, and a low-carbon steel with different yield and ultimate stress.
figures.learnerAction: Increase the load and watch the point travel the curve.

figures.shows: Three stress-strain curves (steel, glass, rubber) on the same axes with areas shaded.

lessons.title: Bonds, density and the four families
lessons.objective: Link bonding to the properties of metals, ceramics and polymers and compare materials by specific stiffness.

concepts.title: Bonding
concepts.summary: Metallic, ionic, covalent and van der Waals bonds set stiffness, melting point and brittleness.

concepts.title: Specific stiffness
concepts.summary: Young's modulus divided by density, a measure of stiffness for a given mass.

misconceptions: Learners think strong bonds mean tough materials. Ceramics have strong bonds and break easily.
Learners expect aluminium to be much stiffer per kilogram than steel; the ratio is almost the same.
Learners assume plastics are weak by nature; fibre-reinforced plastics are among the strongest per mass.
sequence: Four families: metals, ceramics, polymers, composites.
Why metals bend: layers slip, free electrons hold them together.
Why ceramics shatter, why polymers are soft and low in melting point.
Density and specific stiffness: steel 26.8, aluminium 25.9, titanium 25.8 GPa per g/cm^3.
So choosing aluminium for stiffness saves little; shape does the work.
examples: Steel E=210 GPa, density 7.85: 26.8. Aluminium 70, 2.70: 25.9. Titanium 116, 4.5: 25.8.
Nylon: E about 3 GPa, density 1.14: 2.6, about a tenth of metals.
Glass-fibre composite: E about 40 GPa, density 1.9: 21.

figures.shows: Bar chart of E, density and E/density for six materials.
Atoms in a metal lattice sliding versus ionic crystal layers shifting and repelling.
figures.learnerAction: Tap Shear to apply a push.

lessons.title: Why metals are weaker than their bonds
lessons.objective: Explain how dislocations, grain size, alloying and work hardening change strength.

concepts.title: Dislocation
concepts.summary: A line defect whose motion lets metal layers slip one atom row at a time, so metals yield far below ideal strength.

concepts.title: Hall-Petch relation
concepts.summary: Yield strength rises as grain size falls: s = s0 + k/sqrt(d).

misconceptions: Learners think plastic deformation moves whole planes at once. It moves a defect.
Learners think bigger grains mean stronger metal; smaller grains block dislocations.
Learners think work hardening makes metal tougher; it raises strength and lowers ductility.
sequence: Ideal strength is about E/10; real metals yield at E/1000.
Dislocations move easily; every obstacle raises strength.
Solute atoms, precipitates, work hardening: four obstacles.
Cost: strength gained usually costs ductility.
examples: Illustrative constants s0=50 MPa, k=20 MPa*mm^0.5: d=0.01 mm gives 250 MPa; d=0.0025 mm gives 450 MPa.
A copper wire drawn through dies hardens and becomes brittle; annealing it makes it soft again.
Brass: zinc atoms in copper raise yield above pure copper.

figures.shows: A row of atoms with an edge dislocation moving across the crystal under shear, then meeting a grain boundary.
Yield strength against 1/sqrt(grain size) as a straight line.

questionPlan.sample: s0=50 MPa, k=20 MPa*mm^0.5, d=0.04 mm. Yield strength in MPa?
Cold-working a metal does what to its ductility?
Which restores softness after cold work?

historyNotes: E. O. Hall (1951) and N. J. Petch (1953) published the grain-size relation separately.

lessons.title: Steel, carbon and heat treatment
lessons.objective: Use the iron-carbon diagram's lever rule and say what quenching and tempering do.

concepts.title: Eutectoid steel
concepts.summary: Steel with about 0.76 percent carbon turns wholly to pearlite when cooled slowly through 727 C.

concepts.title: Martensite
concepts.summary: Fast quenching traps carbon in a strained, very hard structure; tempering trades some hardness for toughness.

misconceptions: Learners think steel is one material. Carbon content and heat treatment can change its strength severalfold.
Learners think quenching makes the steel tougher. It makes it harder and more brittle until tempered.
Learners misread the lever rule, using the near arm for the fraction of that phase; use the far arm.
sequence: Iron is soft; carbon in solution strengthens it.
Reading the diagram: ferrite, austenite, cementite.
Slow cool gives ferrite and pearlite; the lever rule gives fractions.
Where each is used: blade, spring, gear, structural beam.
examples: 0.40 percent C just below 727 C: pearlite fraction (0.40-0.022)/(0.76-0.022)=0.512.
Chef's knife quenched and tempered at 200 C keeps hardness; at 500 C it becomes tough but softer.

figures.learnerAction: Drag the composition and the cursor; phases label themselves.

lessons.title: Polymers, ceramics and composites
lessons.objective: Compute a fibre composite's stiffness along and across the fibres and explain glass transition.

concepts.title: Glass transition
concepts.summary: Below Tg a polymer is hard and glassy; above it, soft and rubbery.

concepts.title: Rule of mixtures
concepts.summary: Along the fibres, Ec = Vf Ef + (1-Vf) Em; across, 1/Ec = Vf/Ef + (1-Vf)/Em.

misconceptions: Learners assume composites are equally strong in all directions; they are strongly directional.
Learners think thermoplastic and thermoset differ only by name. Thermoplastics remelt; thermosets cross-link.
Learners think ceramics are weak. In compression they are strong; flaws govern tension.
sequence: Ceramics: strong in compression, flaw-controlled in tension.
Rule of mixtures along and across.
examples: Carbon fibre 230 GPa, epoxy 3 GPa, 60 percent fibre: along 139.2 GPa; across 7.36 GPa.
A shopping bag is thermoplastic polyethylene; a cured epoxy cannot be melted.
Window glass fails in tension from surface flaws; thick glass blocks bear compression.

figures.shows: Fibres in a matrix with load arrows along and across the fibres.
Modulus of a polymer against temperature with a drop at Tg.

lessons.title: Fracture, cracks and toughness
lessons.objective: Compute the stress at which a crack of given size grows and say why brittle fracture surprises.

concepts.title: Fracture toughness
concepts.summary: K_IC is the stress intensity at which a crack grows; K = Y s sqrt(pi a).

concepts.title: Ductile-brittle transition
concepts.summary: Many steels turn brittle below a transition temperature, so a crack runs without yielding first.

misconceptions: Learners think a stronger material is safer. High-strength materials can have low toughness.
Learners think a small crack is harmless. Critical stress falls with the square root of crack length.
Learners think brittle failure is slow.
sequence: Stress concentration at a crack tip.
Material property K_IC gives a critical stress or critical crack size.
Plastic zone: ductile materials blunt cracks.
examples: K_IC=50 MPa*sqrt(m), Y=1, crack 2 mm: critical stress = 50/sqrt(pi*0.002)=631 MPa.
Under stress 400 MPa: critical crack a = (50/400)^2/pi = 4.97 mm.
Welded Liberty ships cracked in cold seas in 1940s.

figures.shows: Critical stress against crack length for three toughness values.
Plate with crack and stress lines bunching at the tip.

historyNotes: Brittle failures of welded Liberty ships in World War II led to toughness testing standards.

lessons.title: Corrosion
lessons.objective: Explain corrosion as a cell, predict galvanic pairs, and compute metal loss from current.

concepts.title: Galvanic corrosion
concepts.summary: When two metals touch in an electrolyte, the more reactive one corrodes.

concepts.title: Faraday's law
concepts.summary: Mass lost m = I t M/(n F), with F = 96485 C/mol.

misconceptions: Learners think rust is oxidation by air alone. It needs an electrolyte too.
Learners think paint stops corrosion permanently. A scratch can let corrosion run beneath.
Learners think the nobler metal is damaged.
sequence: Crevice and pitting corrosion in practice.
examples: Galvanised steel: zinc coating corrodes first even where scratched.
Aluminium rivets in steel plate in salt spray.

figures.shows: Two-metal cell in saltwater with electrons and ions drawn.
Galvanic series with order, learner picks which of a pair corrodes.

lessons.title: Casting
lessons.objective: Predict solidification time and pattern size for a casting.

concepts.title: Chvorinov's rule
concepts.summary: Solidification time t = B (V/A)^2, with V volume and A cooling surface area.

concepts.title: Shrinkage
concepts.summary: Metal contracts when it solidifies and cools, so patterns are made oversize.

misconceptions: Learners think a bigger casting freezes in proportion to its size. It goes with the square of the V/A ratio.
Learners think the riser can be smaller than the casting section; it must freeze last.
Learners ignore shrinkage after solidification.
sequence: Defects: shrinkage voids, porosity, cold shuts.
Choosing sand, die or investment casting.
examples: Cube 100 mm: V/A=16.7 mm; cube 50 mm: V/A=8.33 mm, so one quarter the time.
Part 490 mm that shrinks 2 percent: pattern 490/0.98=500 mm.
Die casting aluminium suits thousands of parts; sand suits one-offs.

lessons.title: Forging, rolling and bending
lessons.objective: Compute true strain, forging force and sheet-bend allowance, and tell hot from cold working.

concepts.title: True strain
concepts.summary: e = ln(h0/h1) for a thickness reduction; true strains add.

concepts.title: Hot and cold working
concepts.summary: Working above roughly 0.4 of the melting temperature in kelvin recrystallises the grains as they form.

misconceptions: Learners add percentage reductions rather than true strains.
Learners think forging cuts material; the volume is constant.
Learners think a bent part stays at the die angle; it springs back.
sequence: Force F = flow stress x area.
Hot versus cold: strength, finish, grain.
Sheet bending: bend allowance and springback.
Pick: forging for strength, rolling for plate, extrusion for profiles.
examples: Rolling from 20 mm to 15 mm: e=ln(20/15)=0.288.
Flow stress 250 MPa on 2000 mm^2: 500 kN.
Bend allowance, R=3 mm, t=2 mm, K=0.33, 90 degrees: (pi/2)(3+0.66)=5.75 mm.

figures.shows: Billet being rolled and forged with volume preserved.

lessons.title: Machining
lessons.objective: Calculate cutting speed, material-removal rate, cutting power and the effect of speed on tool life.

concepts.title: Material removal rate
concepts.summary: In turning, MRR = v f d, the product of cutting speed, feed and depth of cut.

concepts.title: Taylor tool life
concepts.summary: V T^n = C: raising cutting speed shortens tool life sharply.

misconceptions: Learners expect faster cutting to be cheaper per part; tool wear rises faster than output.
Learners confuse feed with speed.
Learners think finish depends only on speed; the nose radius and feed set theoretical roughness.
sequence: Cutting speed v = pi D N.
Power = MRR x specific cutting energy.
examples: D=50 mm, 600 rpm: v=94.2 m/min.
Feed 0.2 mm/rev, depth 2 mm: MRR=37.7 cm^3/min=628 mm^3/s; at 3 J/mm^3 that is 1.88 kW.
Taylor n=0.25: speed +20 percent gives tool life x 1.2^-4=0.48. Ra with f=0.2 and nose 0.8 mm: 1.56 micrometres.

lessons.title: Moulding, printing and cost per part
lessons.objective: Compute injection-moulding clamp force and the volume at which tooling pays back.

concepts.title: Clamp force
concepts.summary: Mould halves are held shut against cavity pressure x projected area.

concepts.title: Break-even volume
concepts.summary: Tooling cost divided by the saving per part.

misconceptions: Learners think 3D printing is cheap at scale; per-part cost stays flat.
Learners think moulds are expensive per part; the cost is up front.
Learners forget draft and uniform wall thickness.
sequence: Additive: layers, no tooling, freedom of shape.
examples: Tooling 20000, moulded 1.50, printed 12: break-even 20000/10.5=1905.
Draft of 1 degree on a 40 mm wall moves the face by 0.70 mm.

lessons.title: Holding tolerance in production
lessons.objective: Compute Cp and Cpk and decide whether a process meets a tolerance.

concepts.title: Process capability
concepts.summary: Cp = (USL - LSL)/(6 sigma): how much room the spec has against process spread.

concepts.title: Cpk
concepts.summary: Cpk = min(USL - mean, mean - LSL)/(3 sigma): capability with centring included.

misconceptions: Learners think Cp>1 means every part is good; an off-centre process can still fail.
Learners think measuring more parts changes capability.
Learners treat tolerance and sigma as the same.
examples: A Cpk of 1.0 means about 0.27 percent out of spec if centred.

lessons.title: Choosing a material and a process
lessons.objective: Rank materials with a performance index and match process to shape, volume and material.

concepts.title: Performance index
concepts.summary: A combination of properties that one number ranks; for a light stiff beam, maximise sqrt(E)/density.

concepts.title: Process fit
concepts.summary: A process suits a combination of shape, size, material, volume and tolerance.

misconceptions: Learners rank by the single best property.
Learners forget cost and recyclability.
Learners choose process after material; they interact.
sequence: Compute for steel, aluminium, CFRP, pine.
examples: Index sqrt(E)/density with E in GPa and density in g/cm^3: steel (210, 7.85) 1.85; aluminium (70, 2.70) 3.10; CFRP (100, 1.55) 6.45; pine (10, 0.5) 6.32.
Equal-stiffness beam: aluminium mass is 0.60 of steel.
Galvanic corrosion forbids aluminium rivets in steel.
